subject: Near-miss overload event (Jan 12) — timeline, risk reduction, rollout confidence

From: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwoodinference.com>

Date: Mon, Jan 12, 2025 at 8:34 AM PT
Subject: Near-miss overload event (Jan 12) — timeline, risk reduction, rollout confidence

Lauren, Nikhil —

I’m getting pinged by leadership this morning after the near-miss overnight (capacity dip + retry storm). I need a crisp write-up I can forward.

Can you send by EOD (preferably by 2pm PT):
1) Timeline (what happened, when, what we did, current status)
2) Risk reduction summary (what’s changed already vs. what’s still open)
3) Rollout confidence for hot-route capacity protection (what’s the realistic timeline, what are the biggest risks, what’s our rollback plan)

Keep it very concrete (bullets). Assume the audience is exec staff / not deep in the details.

Thanks,
Neha

—

From: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwoodinference.com>
To: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: Nikhil Sharma <nikhil.sharma@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Mon, Jan 12, 2025 at 9:07 AM PT
Subject: Re: Near-miss overload event (Jan 12) — timeline, risk reduction, rollout confidence

Neha —

Initial bullets below (I’ll refine once I get the final incident notes from SRE, but this is directionally accurate).

1) Timeline (PT)
- 00:41–00:47: Brief regional capacity dip (GPU fleet degradation) + elevated retries from a small number of high-traffic routes.
- 00:48: p99 latency spikes on top enterprise endpoints; error rate started to trend up but did not breach enterprise availability SLO (near-miss).
- 00:52: On-call identified saturation on the “hot routes” (high QPS + long contexts) driving disproportionate queue depth.
- 00:55: Mitigation: manual routing policy adjustment + temporary tightening of burst allowance for self-serve traffic in affected region.
- 01:06: Latency recovers; by ~01:20 metrics stable. Continued monitoring through ~03:00.
- Current status: stable; no ongoing customer impact beyond brief latency degradation. Support has 1 inbound question about intermittent 429s (we expect more questions once customers look at logs).

2) Risk reduction summary
- What worked:
  - Manual intervention successfully protected enterprise traffic at the expense of lower-tier throughput (desired outcome).
  - Existing safeguards prevented a fleet-wide cascading failure.
- What remains risky:
  - The behavior is not yet “predictable/explainable” to customers when we tighten limits under pressure (inconsistent 429 semantics across gateway/router paths).
  - Config propagation + enforcement is still too manual; we’re relying on on-call judgement instead of policy-based admission control.
  - We don’t have consistent per-route/per-tier saturation signals surfaced in one place (we stitched together multiple dashboards).

3) Rollout confidence / plan (hot-route capacity protection)
- We can credibly reduce the risk of recurrence once tier-aware admission control + enterprise lanes are on by default for top routes.
- Realistic timeline (high level):
  - This week: finalize standard 429 payload + Retry-After semantics; lock initial “top routes” list; finish alert tuning for throttling spikes.
  - Next 2 weeks: staged rollout by region via feature flags; start with canary tenants; game day + load tests as gates.
- Rollback plan:
  - Kill-switch at gateway/router to disable new enforcement policies if we see false positives / widespread throttling.

I’ll send a tighter version after Nikhil adds Hosted-facing semantics + customer messaging risks.

-Lauren

Lauren Bishop
Product (Enterprise/Dedicated)
Redwood Inference

From: Nikhil Sharma <nikhil.sharma@redwoodinference.com>

Subject: Re: Near-miss overload event (Jan 12) — timeline, risk reduction, rollout confidence

Adding Hosted-API lens + “confidence” framing.

Customer-facing impact (Hosted)
- Customers saw: brief tail latency increase; a small number may have seen elevated 429s during the mitigation window.
- The bigger issue is predictability: today, 429s can be returned from different layers with slightly different payloads/reason codes, which makes client behavior (retries/backoff) worse during overload.

Risk reduction — what will materially change with hot-route protection
- Clear, consistent overload semantics:
  - Standardized 429 + Retry-After across gateway and router.
  - Reason codes that distinguish “rate limit”, “quota”, and “temporary capacity protection” (so clients can back off instead of retry storming).
- Priority routing:
  - Enterprise routes get an explicit admission lane; self-serve traffic is shed first during saturation.
  - “Bounded fairness” so we avoid permanent starvation but still preserve enterprise SLOs.
- Better operators’ signals:
  - Per-route/per-tier throttle rate + lane utilization + saturation indicators (queue depth/prefill saturation) in a single dashboard.

Rollout confidence (my view)
- Medium-high once we finish two things:
  1) Standardized 429 behavior (so we don’t create a new support fire)
  2) Cardinality-safe metrics/alerts (so on-call can trust the signals)
- Biggest risk: false positive throttling due to noisy backpressure signals or mis-tuned thresholds. That’s why we should treat the first rollout as “canary + rapid rollback” rather than a hard launch.

For your forwardable summary, I’d suggest a simple message:
- “We had a near-miss; mitigation held; the long-term fix is tier-aware admission control and enterprise priority lanes; rollout is staged with a kill-switch.”

-Nikhil

Nikhil Sharma
Product, Hosted API
Redwood Inference

Neha — here’s a forward-ready version.

EXEC SUMMARY — Near-miss overload event (Jan 12, PT)

Did we breach enterprise SLOs?
- No breach observed. We saw a short p99 latency spike on a small set of endpoints; availability SLO remained within budget.

Are there active escalations?
- No active exec escalation. Support has one inquiry (not a major incident), and we expect follow-up questions as customers review logs.

Timeline (PT)
- 00:41: Regional capacity dip begins; load increases on a small set of high-traffic endpoints.
- 00:48: Tail latency rises on top enterprise routes.
- 00:52: On-call confirms overload concentrated in a few “hot routes.”
- 00:55: Mitigation applied (temporary traffic shaping + routing policy adjustment to prioritize enterprise).
- 01:06: Latency returns to normal range; continued monitoring.
- ~01:20: System stable.

What reduces risk in the next 7 days
- Standardize overload responses:
  - Consistent 429 payload + Retry-After guidance across gateway/router (reduces retry storms and support burden).
- Tighten operational visibility:
  - Single dashboard for per-route/per-tier throttling rate + lane utilization + saturation signals.
  - Alert tuning to page on sustained enterprise-lane degradation (not on planned load tests).
- Canary enablement:
  - Feature-flagged rollout in one region for a small set of canary tenants.

What we expect within 30 days
- Tier-aware admission control is enabled for the initial “top enterprise routes” across regions (staged rollout).
- Enterprise “priority lane” routing on by default for those routes, with bounded fairness for lower tiers.
- Load-test + game day gates to validate behavior under burst + retry-storm scenarios prior to broader enablement.

Top risks / what could cause slip
1) Mis-tuned thresholds/backpressure signals causing false positive throttling (customer-visible 429s)
2) Metrics/label cardinality issues impacting dashboard performance or alert reliability

Mitigation / rollback
- Rollout is staged and guarded by feature flags.
- Kill-switch exists to disable new enforcement policies if we detect widespread throttling or incorrect classification.

References (internal)
- Linear program tracker: ENG-4821
- Load test gates: ENG-4829
- Runbook: overload throttling & priority routing response

If you want, I can also provide a one-liner for customer-facing comms (Hosted vs Dedicated) but I assume you just need the internal readout.

-Lauren
